newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Bosnian Serb police shut down opposition radio.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian Serb police shut down opposition radio.

text.p: Bosnian Serb police on Wednesday shut down the last of the independent radio stations which backed dismissed army commander General Ratko Mladic.
"Between 14.00 and 15:00 today, police forcibly switched off and seized the transmitter used by Radio Krajina, putting an end to the last remaining vestige of free speech," the radio said.
The closure is another incident in a war of nerves between the ousted general and civilian authorities dating back to early 1995.

Bosnian Serb president Biljana Plavsic dismissed Bosnian Serb army (BSA) commander Mladic and his wartime general staff last weekend in an attempt by the government to regain civilian control over the BSA.
But Mladic, indicted twice by an international war crimes tribunal in The Hague, resisted the dismissal.
Diplomats believe Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic backed the BSA purge as he strives to distance himself from wartime allies in his new pursuit of peace in the Balkans and acceptance overseas.
Analysts describe Mladic as an unpredictable liability now that the peace process has entered its second year.
Mladic, a tough professional soldier, always jibbed at taking orders from the civilians and refused to obey even his paymasters in Belgrade on several occasions.
Radio Krajina, based in the BSA command in Banja Luka, has infuriated civilian authorities in Pale.
It started broadcasting as Moslem and Croats swept over western Bosnia in the summer of 1995, at the height of a war of words between ousted leader Radovan Karadzic and Mladic.

Its origins stemmed from the army's fury at Karadzic's attempts to blame it for military defeats and his first attempt to sack Mladic which ended in humiliation after the entire command staff rebelled.
The Serb leadership and the army split irrevocably early last year when the politicians refused to give Mladic the martial law powers he said he needed.
Radio Krajina used phone-in programmes to denounce government tactics that alienated former allies in Belgrade, provoked NATO bombing and led to big military defeats.
"The fall of Radio Krajina shows the civilian authorities have finally won the upper hand," one diplomat said.
